records.content:
How does learning rate affect the training of a small CNN?

Imagine teaching a computer to recognize different types of clothing. At first, it will make mistakes. As it learns, it adjusts its values to make better predictions. But how much should it adjust each time?

This is where the learning rate comes in. It controls how big or small the adjustments are during training. If the adjustments are too small, learning can take longer. If they are too large, the model may struggle to learn properly.

In this experiment, we wanted to find out: How does learning rate change the training curve of a small CNN, and where does training become unstable?

To answer this, we’ll tested five different learning rates using the Fashion-MNIST dataset.

A neural network learns by adjusting values inside the model called weights and biases. These values help the model recognize patterns and make predictions.

Think of it like walking toward a destination. If your steps are too small, you will take longer to reach it. If your steps are too big, you might go past the destination. The same idea applies to learning rate.

During training, the model follows these steps:

It makes a prediction.

It checks how wrong the prediction is using a loss function.

It calculates a gradient to determine how the model’s values should change.

It updates its weights and biases to improve its next prediction.

A simplified formula for updating a weight is:w_{\text{new}} = w_{\text{old}} - \alpha \times \text{gradient}

Where:

w_{\text{old}} is the current weight.

\alpha is the learning rate.

The gradient indicates how the weight should change.

w_{\text{new}} is the updated weight.

Here, the learning rate is represented by \alpha. It controls how big the adjustment will be.

In this experiment we will be using Adam as the optimizer. An optimizer is the method that updates the model’s weights and biases during training. Adam uses information from current and previous gradients to guide its updates. The learning rate is a separate setting that controls the overall size of those updates.

Training is considered more stable when the model improves consistently. For example, when the loss decreases over time, it is usually a good sign. However, when the loss keeps increasing or changing sharply, it may mean that the learning rate is not suitable.

For this experiment, we will used Fashion-MNIST, a dataset containing grayscale images of clothing. Each image is 28 × 28 pixels and belongs to one of 10 clothing categories.

Using a small Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to classify the images. A CNN is useful for image tasks because it can learn patterns such as shapes, edges, and other visual features.

To see how learning rate affects training, let’s test five different values:

Only the learning rate changed. The other settings stayed the same so that the comparison would be fair.

This experiment used 10,000 images for training and 6,000 images for validation. Each model was trained for four epochs with a batch size of 64.

We also used three random seeds: 42, 43, and 44. This means each learning rate was tested three times. Doing this helps check whether the results stay similar or change depending on the random starting values.

In total, there were 15 runs: five learning rates tested across three seeds.

After running the experiments, we compared the training loss, validation loss, training accuracy, and validation accuracy.

The table below shows the average results from the three runs. The values after ± show how much the results varied across the seeds.

records.content:
The results show that changing the learning rate affected how quickly the model learned and how consistent its performance was.

The smallest learning rate, 0.00001, still improved during training. However, it finished with 78.30% average validation accuracy. This suggests that its updates were too small to reach the same performance as the other better-performing settings within four epochs.

The 0.0001 and 0.001 learning rates gave the best results. Among the five values, 0.001 performed the best, reaching 88.47% average validation accuracy and 0.3148 average validation loss. Its results were also fairly consistent across the three runs.

The 0.01 learning rate also learned, but its average validation accuracy was lower at 84.98%. Its results also varied more than those of 0.0001 and 0.001.

The largest learning rate, 0.1, showed the clearest warning signs. Two of its three runs ended with validation accuracy close to 10%, while the third reached 73.13%. Since Fashion-MNIST has 10 categories, an accuracy close to 10% is similar to guessing.

However, none of the runs produced non-finite loss values such as NaN. So, it would not be correct to say that all three runs completely failed or numerically diverged. Instead, the results show that 0.1 was unreliable for this particular experiment.

Overall, the findings support the idea that a learning rate that is too small can slow down learning, while one that is too large can make training inconsistent.

Limitations

There are also some limitations to this experiment. Only 10,000 training images and 6,000 validation images were used instead of the full dataset. The model was also trained for only four epochs, so some learning rates might have performed differently with more training time.

Another limitation is that the experiment used only one CNN architecture and the Adam optimizer. Other models or optimizers may produce different results. Although three random seeds were tested, they are still not enough to make strong statistical claims.

Because of these limitations, the results only show what happened with this particular setup. They do not mean that 0.001 will always be the best learning rate for every CNN.

Learning rate matters. It controls how big the model’s adjustments are during training. This can affect how quickly the model learns.

A bigger learning rate is not always better. In this experiment, 0.1 produced inconsistent results, while 0.001 gave the best average validation performance.

It is important to compare multiple runs. Testing different seeds helped show that the same learning rate can produce different results. Looking at only one run may give a misleading impression.

The workflow includes creating a custom PyTorch Dataset, using a DataLoader to load the images in batches, running five pre-trained models on the dataset, and comparing their performance using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.

records.content:
Each image is processed using the preprocessing required by the current model. Since the dataset contains only laptops and cell phones, the model compares its scores for the two corresponding ImageNet classes: laptop (620) and cellular telephone (487). The class with the higher score is used as the prediction.

The pre-trained models normally predict among 1000 ImageNet classes. For this activity, only the two relevant classes—laptop (620) and cellular telephone (487)—are considered. The model compares the scores of these two classes, and the one with the higher score becomes the predicted label. This allows the pre-trained models to be used directly on the custom dataset without additional training.

all_results = {}

for model_name, (model_fn, weights) in model_configs.items():
    print(f"Running {model_name}...")
    model = model_fn(weights=weights)
    model.eval()
    transform = weights.transforms()

    records = []
    for images, labels in dataloader:
        for img, true_label in zip(images, labels):
            x = transform(img).unsqueeze(0)
            with torch.no_grad():
                logits = model(x)

            laptop_score = logits[0, LAPTOP_IDX].item()
            phone_score = logits[0, PHONE_IDX].item()
            predicted_label = 0 if laptop_score > phone_score else 1

            records.append({
                "True Label": true_label,
                "Predicted Label": predicted_label,
                "Correct": true_label == predicted_label
            })

    all_results[model_name] = pd.DataFrame(records)

print("\nInference complete for all 5 models.")

records.content:
The five pre-trained models were evaluated on the custom dataset using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The resulting values are shown in the comparison table and chart above.

Since the inference process compares only the scores of the two selected ImageNet classes (see the methodology note above), every image is assigned to either laptop or cell phone, with no option for the model to predict anything else. Therefore, the reported metrics reflect each model’s ability to distinguish between these two specific classes, rather than its full 1000-class ImageNet classification performance. Any misclassification or recall error means that the model’s score for the incorrect one of these two classes happened to be higher; it does not mean that the model recognized the image as something entirely unrelated.

The models produced different results on this particular dataset. The comparison table and visualization show the observed differences in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score across the five models. Differences in performance across the five models may be related to several factors:

Model architecture: The five models use different architectures, which may affect how they represent and classify visual features. These architectural differences may contribute to differences in performance on the custom dataset.

Model complexity: More complex models may capture more detailed visual features, but they can also require more computational resources. Simpler models may have different performance characteristics and may be more practical when computational resources are limited.

Preprocessing requirements: Each model expects a specific input size and normalization, handled here through each model’s own weights.transforms(). Differences in how sensitive a model is to image quality, lighting, or background may still affect its predictions even when preprocessing is handled correctly.

Similarity to ImageNet’s original training data: Since all five models were pretrained on ImageNet’s natural, real-world photos, a model’s performance may depend on how visually similar the custom dataset’s images are to typical ImageNet photos, versus more stylized, product-photo-style images.

Important limitation: This dataset contains only 3 images per class (6 images total). With such a small sample size, a single misclassification changes accuracy by roughly 16.7 percentage points. This means a result such as “100% accuracy” should be understood specifically as 100% accuracy on this particular 6-image custom dataset, and not interpreted as a general claim about that model’s real-world accuracy. A larger and more varied dataset would be needed to draw more reliable conclusions about how the models perform on a broader set of images.

Conclusion: This exercise demonstrates how pre-trained image classification models can be applied directly to a custom dataset without additional training when the target categories are available in the models’ original class set. Because the dataset contains only six images, the results should be interpreted as observations from this particular dataset rather than as a general measure of model performance. Any comparison between the models should therefore be limited to the dataset and conditions tested in this activity.

This notebook contains basic concepts in deep learning. It covers a simple neural network forward pass, error calculation, backpropagation, and a linear regression model implemented using PyTorch.

These sections include the concepts, calculations, code, and explanations needed to understand each task.

An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is a type of model made up of connected artificial neurons, or units, that are organized into layers. A typical ANN has an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer.

The input layer receives the data, while the hidden layers process and transform the information. The output layer then produces the final result. Connections between neurons have weights, which determine how much influence an input has on the calculation. Biases are also added during the calculations, and activation functions help determine the output of each neuron.

During training, the network uses examples from a dataset to learn patterns. Its output is compared with the expected result, and the error can be used to adjust the weights through backpropagation.

A feedforward neural network is one of the simplest types of artificial neural networks. In this type of network, information moves in one direction, starting from the input layer and passing through the hidden layers until it reaches the output layer.

The values are processed at each layer using weights, biases, and activation functions. This forward movement of information is called a forward pass or forward propagation.
A forward pass (also called forward propagation) is the process where input data flows through a neural network from the input layer to the output layer to generate a prediction.

Data Flow: Data moves forward through the network, passing through the hidden layers until it reaches the output layer.

Calculations: At each layer, neurons multiply the inputs by their weights, add a bias, and apply an activation function such as ReLU or Sigmoid.

No Learning: During the forward pass, the weights and biases remain unchanged. The network only uses them to calculate the output.

Error Calculation: After the output is produced, it can be compared with the target value to determine the error.

The results from the forward pass and loss calculation are then used during backpropagation to calculate the gradients. An optimizer can use these gradients to update the network’s weights and biases.

Instruction: Perform a single forward pass and compute for the error.

x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}y = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix}f=max(0, Z_n)\text{hidden unit weights} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
w_{11} = 0.2 && w_{12} = -0.3 \\
w_{13} = 0.4 && w_{14} = 0.1 \\
w_{15} = -0.5 && w_{16} = 0.2
\end{bmatrix}\text{output unit weights} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
w_{21} = -0.3 \\
w_{22} = -0.2
\end{bmatrix}\theta = 
\begin{bmatrix}
\theta_{1} = -0.4 \\
\theta_{2} = 0.2 \\
\theta_{3} = 0.1
\end{bmatrix}

import numpy as np



x = np.array([1, 0, 1], dtype=float)
y = np.array([1.0])

w_hidden = np.array([
    [0.2, -0.3],
    [0.4,  0.1],
    [-0.5, 0.2],
])
theta_hidden = np.array([-0.4, 0.2])

w_output = np.array([[-0.3], [-0.2]])
theta_output = np.array([0.1])

def relu(z):
    return np.maximum(0, z)



# Forward pass
Z_hidden = x.dot(w_hidden) + theta_hidden
H = relu(Z_hidden)
Z_output = H.dot(w_output) + theta_output
y_hat = relu(Z_output)

print(f"Z1 = {Z_hidden[0]:.4f}, Z2 = {Z_hidden[1]:.4f}")
print(f"H1 = {H[0]:.4f}, H2 = {H[1]:.4f}")
print(f"Z3 = {Z_output[0]:.4f}")
print(f"y_hat = {y_hat[0]:.4f}")

# Error
error = y_hat - y
sq_error = (y - y_hat)**2
print(f"\nError (y_hat - y) = {error[0]:.4f}")
print(f"Squared Error = {sq_error[0]:.4f}")



The input values are first passed through the hidden layer using the given weights and biases. This produces Z1 = -0.7 and Z2 = 0.1. Applying the ReLU activation function changes Z1 to 0 while Z2 remains 0.1, giving H1 = 0 and H2 = 0.1.

The hidden-layer outputs are then passed to the output layer, producing Z3 = 0.08. Since the value is positive, ReLU keeps it as 0.08, which becomes the predicted output.

The target value is 1, while the prediction is only 0.08, so the prediction is lower than the target. Using the error calculation ŷ - y, the error is -0.92. The squared error is 0.8464.

Backpropagation, also called backward propagation or backprop, is a fundamental process used to train artificial neural networks. It calculates how the error affects the network’s weights and biases through gradients, which are then used to update the parameters.

Forward Pass: Input data moves through the network layers. Neurons use weights, biases, and activation functions to generate a prediction.

Error Calculation: The predicted output is compared with the actual target value to determine the error.

Backward Pass: The process starts at the output layer and moves backward through the network. It uses the chain rule to calculate how each weight and bias contributes to the error.

Parameter Update: The gradients calculated during backpropagation are combined with the learning rate to update the weights and biases.

This process can be repeated during training, allowing the network to gradually improve its predictions.

Instruction: Perform a forward and backward propagation in python using the inputs from Laboratory Task 2x = np.array([1, 0, 1])
y = np.array([1])

# use relu as the activation function.

# learning rate
lr = 0.001

# Learning rate
lr = 0.001

# Derivative of ReLU
def relu_derivative(z):
    return (z > 0).astype(float)



# Forward Pass
Z_hidden = x.dot(w_hidden) + theta_hidden
H = relu(Z_hidden)

Z_output = H.dot(w_output) + theta_output
y_hat = relu(Z_output)

error = y_hat - y

print("Hidden weighted sum:", Z_hidden)
print("Hidden output:", H)
print("Output weighted sum:", Z_output)
print("Predicted output:", y_hat)
print("Error:", error)



# Backward Pass
delta_output = error * relu_derivative(Z_output)

grad_w_output = H.reshape(-1, 1) * delta_output
grad_theta_output = delta_output

delta_hidden = (
    w_output.flatten() * delta_output[0]
    * relu_derivative(Z_hidden)
)

grad_w_hidden = np.outer(x, delta_hidden)
grad_theta_hidden = delta_hidden

# Update Parameters
w_output = w_output - lr * grad_w_output
theta_output = theta_output - lr * grad_theta_output

w_hidden = w_hidden - lr * grad_w_hidden
theta_hidden = theta_hidden - lr * grad_theta_hidden

print("\nUpdated hidden weights:")
print(w_hidden)
print("\nUpdated output weights:")
print(w_output)
print("\nUpdated hidden biases:")
print(theta_hidden)
print("\nUpdated output bias:")
print(theta_output)



The forward pass first produces the same values as the previous activity. The hidden-layer weighted sums are -0.7 and 0.1, which become 0 and 0.1 after applying ReLU. The output of the network is 0.08, while the target value is 1, resulting in an error of -0.92.

During backpropagation, the error is propagated backward through the output and hidden layers. The ReLU derivative is used to calculate the gradients for the network’s weights and biases.

Because H1 was inactive after the ReLU function changed its value to 0, the parameters connected to H1 did not receive an update in this step. H2 was active, so the parameters connected to H2 were updated.

The calculated gradients are then used to update the weights and biases using the learning rate of 0.001. The updated parameters are slightly different from their original values. These updates are intended to move the network’s prediction closer to the target value in the next forward pass.
PyTorch is an open-source framework used for building and training machine learning and deep learning models. In this activity, PyTorch is used to implement and train a linear regression model.

For the linear regression example, the following PyTorch components are used:

Input and Target: The input data and expected target values are defined for the model.

Dataset and DataLoader: The dataset stores the samples and their corresponding targets, while the DataLoader provides the data in batches during training.

nn.Linear: A fully connected layer used to connect the input and output features of the model. Two nn.Linear layers are used in the regression model.

Loss Function: Measures the difference between the model’s predictions and the target values.

Optimizer: Uses the calculated gradients to update the model’s parameters.

Training: The model repeatedly processes the data, calculates the loss, and updates its parameters to improve its predictions.

Linear regression is used to model the relationship between input variables and continuous output values. In this activity, PyTorch is used to build and train a simple linear regression model.

The dataset contains three input variables: temperature, rainfall, and humidity. The model uses these values to predict two target values: apples and oranges.

The model is trained using Mean Squared Error (MSE) as the loss function and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) as the optimizer.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader



# Dataset
x_train = np.array([
    [73, 67, 43], [91, 88, 64], [87, 134, 58],
    [102, 43, 37], [69, 96, 70], [73, 67, 43],
    [91, 88, 64], [87, 134, 58], [102, 43, 37],
    [69, 96, 70], [73, 67, 43], [91, 88, 64],
    [87, 134, 58], [102, 43, 37], [69, 96, 70]
], dtype='float32')

y_train = np.array([
    [56, 70], [81, 101], [119, 133],
    [22, 37], [103, 119], [56, 70],
    [81, 101], [119, 133], [22, 37],
    [103, 119], [56, 70], [81, 101],
    [119, 133], [22, 37], [103, 119]
], dtype='float32')



# Convert data to PyTorch tensors
inputs = torch.from_numpy(x_train)
targets = torch.from_numpy(y_train)

# Create dataset and DataLoader
train_ds = TensorDataset(inputs, targets)

batch_size = 8
train_dl = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)



# Define the model
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(3, 8),
    nn.Linear(8, 2)
)



# Loss function and optimizer
criterion = nn.MSELoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.00001)



# Training
num_epochs = 1000

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    for xb, yb in train_dl:

        # Forward pass
        predictions = model(xb)

        # Calculate loss
        loss = criterion(predictions, yb)

        # Backward pass
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()

        # Update parameters
        optimizer.step()

    if (epoch + 1) % 100 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch [{epoch + 1}/{num_epochs}], Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")



with torch.no_grad():
    predictions = model(inputs)
    final_loss = criterion(predictions, targets)

print("\nFinal MSE Loss:", final_loss.item())

print("\nPredicted values:")
print(predictions)

print("\nActual values:")
print(targets)



The model was trained using the given regression dataset, where temperature, rainfall, and humidity were used as the input variables and apples and oranges were used as the target values.

The model uses two fully connected layers. The first layer takes the three input features and produces eight intermediate values, while the second layer uses those eight values to produce the two target outputs. During each training step, the model generates predictions, calculates the MSE loss, performs backpropagation, and updates its parameters using SGD.

The training was performed for 1000 epochs with a batch size of 8. The overall decrease in loss during training indicates that the model was adjusting its parameters to make predictions closer to the target values.

The final MSE loss represents the average squared difference between the model’s predictions and the actual target values. A lower MSE indicates that the predictions are closer to the actual values.

The different sections connect to show how a neural network processes data, calculates errors, updates its parameters, and is eventually trained using a framework such as PyTorch.

The forward pass showed how the input values move through the hidden and output layers to produce a prediction. The input values were multiplied by the given weights and combined with the biases to calculate the hidden-layer values. The ReLU activation function then changed the negative value of -0.7 to 0, while the positive value of 0.1 remained unchanged. This resulted in H1 = 0 and H2 = 0.1. The hidden-layer outputs were then passed to the output layer, producing a predicted value of 0.08. Compared with the target value of 1, the prediction resulted in an error of -0.92 and a squared error of 0.8464.

The forward pass also showed how an activation function can affect the rest of the training process. Since the value for H1 was negative before applying ReLU, it became 0 and did not contribute to the output in that forward pass. During backpropagation, the error was passed backward through the network and gradients were calculated using the ReLU derivative. Because H1 was inactive, the parameters connected to it did not receive an update in that step, while the parameters connected to the active hidden unit H2 were updated. The learning rate of 0.001 was then used when updating the weights and biases.

The PyTorch section showed how the same general process can be applied using a framework. The regression model used temperature, rainfall, and humidity as the three input features and predicted apples and oranges as the two target values. The model used two fully connected layers, with the first layer changing the three input features into eight intermediate values and the second layer producing the two outputs. MSE Loss was used to measure the prediction error, while SGD was used to update the model parameters. The model was trained using a batch size of 8 for 1000 epochs.

The choice of learning rate also had a clear effect on the training result. A learning rate of 0.0001 caused the loss to become nan, while the smaller learning rate of 0.00001 allowed the model to train more stably and reach a final MSE loss of about 0.5. This shows that the learning rate controls how much the model’s parameters change during each update, so the value used during training can affect whether the model is able to learn properly.

Overall, the concepts of artificial neural networks, forward propagation, error calculation, backpropagation, and PyTorch training are connected through the same basic learning process. The manual calculations made it possible to see what happens inside the network step by step, while the PyTorch implementation showed how many of these calculations can be handled automatically when training a model.

This notebook covers the fundamentals of working with PyTorch tensors, including converting NumPy arrays into tensors, creating tensors directly, changing data types, reshaping, indexing, and performing arithmetic and matrix operations.

These concepts are applied in Laboratory Task 5, which walks through the process of creating a NumPy array, converting it into a tensor, modifying its shape and type, and performing matrix multiplication with another tensor.

A tensor is a multi-dimensional array, similar to a NumPy ndarray, and is the core data structure used in PyTorch. Tensors are used to store the inputs, outputs, and parameters (weights and biases) of a model.

The main advantage tensors have over regular NumPy arrays is that they can run on a GPU or other specialized hardware, which allows much faster computation, especially for large models.

PyTorch tensors can be created directly from existing NumPy arrays using torch.from_numpy(). This is useful when data has already been loaded or processed using NumPy, since it avoids having to recreate the data manually.

A tensor created this way shares memory with the original NumPy array, and it keeps the same data type (dtype) as the array it came from, unless the type is changed afterward.

Tensors can be reshaped into different dimensions using .reshape(), as long as the total number of elements stays the same. They also support slicing and indexing similar to NumPy arrays, arithmetic operations (such as squaring values with .pow()), and matrix multiplication using functions like torch.mm().

These operations form the basis for how data flows through and is transformed inside a neural network.

Perform Standard Imports

Create a function called set_seed() that accepts seed: int as a parameter, this function must return nothing but just set the seed to a certain value.

Create a NumPy array called "arr" that contains 6 random integers between 0 (inclusive) and 5 (exclusive), call the set_seed() function and use 42 as the seed parameter.

Create a tensor "x" from the array above

Change the dtype of x from int32 to int64

Reshape x into a 3x2 tensor

There are several ways to do this.

Return the right-hand column of tensor x

Without changing x, return a tensor of square values of x

There are several ways to do this.

Create a tensor y with the same number of elements as x, that can be matrix-multiplied with x

Use PyTorch directly (not NumPy) to create a tensor of random integers between 0 (inclusive) and 5 (exclusive). Use 42 as seed.

Think about what shape it should have to permit matrix multiplication.

Step 1 — Standard Imports

import torch
import numpy as np



Step 2 — Define set_seed()

def set_seed(seed):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)



Step 3 — Create array arr

arr = np.random.randint(0, 5, size=6).astype('int32')

assert np.array_equal(arr, np.array([3,4,2,4,4,1])), "Oops"

Step 4 — Convert arr to tensor x

Step 6 — Reshape x into 3x2

assert torch.equal(y, torch.tensor([[2, 2, 1],[4, 1, 0]])), "Oops"
print(y)



Step 10 — Matrix product of x and y

prod = torch.mm(x,y)
prod



Since set_seed(42) is called before every random draw, both arr and y produce the exact same values every time this runs, which is why both assert checks pass. The tensor x starts as a flat 6-element tensor with dtype int32, then gets converted to int64 before being reshaped into a 3x2 matrix. Slicing out the right-hand column doesn’t change x itself, and squaring it with .pow(2) also leaves x unchanged since it returns a new tensor instead of modifying it in place. Since x has shape (3,2), y is created with shape (2,3) so the two can be matrix-multiplied, giving a final 3x3 result.

This task covered the basics of working with tensors in PyTorch, from converting a NumPy array into a tensor to adjusting its type and shape, and finally performing matrix multiplication.

Setting a seed before generating random values made the results reproducible, which is why arr and y matched their expected values in the assertions. Working through the reshaping and slicing steps also showed that operations like .pow() don’t change the original tensor, they return a new one instead — an important detail when writing PyTorch code.

The final matrix multiplication step also showed why tensor shapes matter: x and y needed compatible dimensions (3x2 and 2x3) for torch.mm() to work, producing a 3x3 output. Overall, this task built a solid foundation for tensor creation and manipulation, which are used throughout the rest of building and training neural networks in PyTorch.

A Convolutional Neural Network is commonly used for image-related tasks because it can learn useful features from image data. In the original notebook, the MNIST dataset is used, where each image is a grayscale image with a size of 28 × 28 pixels.

The architecture used in this laboratory activity starts with convolution and pooling layers that extract features from the image. The resulting feature maps are then passed through dropout and fully connected layers before producing the final output for the 10 MNIST digit classes.

A CNN processes an image through several layers. Convolutional layers learn image features, while pooling layers reduce the spatial size of the feature maps. Activation functions such as ReLU are applied after the convolutional and fully connected layers in the given architecture.

For the MNIST input, the first layer receives one channel with a height and width of 28 pixels:ext{Input} = (1, 28, 28)

The architecture uses four convolutional layers and two max-pooling layers. The first pooling layer uses padding of 1, so the 28 × 28 input becomes 15 × 15 after pooling. The second pooling layer reduces the 15 × 15 feature maps to 7 × 7.

The convolutional layers can be created using nn.Conv2d, while the pooling layers use nn.MaxPool2d. The fully connected layers use nn.Linear. A dropout layer with p=0.2 is placed before flattening the feature maps.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

Instruction: Convert the given CNN architecture diagram into a PyTorch CNN Architecture.

The diagram contains four convolutional layers, two max-pooling layers, a dropout layer, three fully connected layers, ReLU activations, and a final SoftMax output.

class CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        # Convolutional layers
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)
        self.pool1 = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=1)

        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)
        self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)
        self.conv4 = nn.Conv2d(128, 256, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)

        self.pool2 = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0)

        # Dropout
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=0.2)

        # Fully connected layers
        self.fcn1 = nn.Linear(256 * 7 * 7, 1000)
        self.fcn2 = nn.Linear(1000, 500)
        self.fcn3 = nn.Linear(500, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = self.pool1(x)

        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x))
        x = F.relu(self.conv3(x))
        x = F.relu(self.conv4(x))
        x = self.pool2(x)

        x = self.dropout(x)

        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)

        x = F.relu(self.fcn1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fcn2(x))
        x = F.softmax(self.fcn3(x), dim=1)

        return x

The class can now be instantiated to create the CNN model.

model = CNN()
model

Since the MNIST input has one channel and a size of 28 × 28, a sample input can be created with the shape (32, 1, 28, 28), where 32 represents the batch size. The final layer should produce 10 outputs, one for each digit from 0 to 9.

sample_input = torch.randn(32, 1, 28, 28)

output = model(sample_input)

print("Input shape:", sample_input.shape)
print("Output shape:", output.shape)

The intermediate shapes can also be checked to make sure that the architecture follows the given diagram. The first pooling layer changes the spatial size from 28 × 28 to 15 × 15 because it uses padding of 1. The second pooling layer then changes 15 × 15 to 7 × 7.

x = F.relu(model.conv1(x))
print("After Conv1:", x.shape)

x = model.pool1(x)
print("After MaxPool1:", x.shape)

x = F.relu(model.conv2(x))
print("After Conv2:", x.shape)

print("After Conv3:", x.shape)

x = F.relu(model.conv4(x))
print("After Conv4:", x.shape)

x = model.pool2(x)
print("After MaxPool2:", x.shape)

x = model.dropout(x)
x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
print("After Flatten:", x.shape)



The CNN was created based on the architecture shown in the diagram. The input is a grayscale MNIST image with one channel and a size of 28 × 28. The first convolutional layer changes the number of channels from 1 to 32 while keeping the spatial size at 28 × 28 because a kernel size of 3 and padding of 1 are used.

The first max-pooling layer reduces the spatial dimensions to 15 × 15. Three more convolutional layers then increase the number of feature channels from 32 to 64, then 128, and finally 256. The second max-pooling layer reduces the feature maps to 7 × 7.

After pooling, dropout with a probability of 0.2 is applied. The feature maps are then flattened into 256 × 7 × 7 = 12,544 values before entering the fully connected layers. The first fully connected layer produces 1,000 values, the second produces 500 values, and the final layer produces 10 outputs. ReLU is used in the hidden layers, while SoftMax is applied to the final output to produce class probabilities for the ten MNIST digits.

Since SoftMax is already applied inside the model, this architecture is meant to be used with a loss function that expects probabilities, such as nn.NLLLoss (combined with a log of the output) rather than nn.CrossEntropyLoss. nn.CrossEntropyLoss already applies SoftMax internally, so combining it with a model that also applies SoftMax would apply it twice, which can affect training. This becomes relevant once this architecture is actually trained in a later activity.

There will always be things that are still unfamiliar, and that is a normal part of learning. Some concepts may be understood quickly, while others may require more time, practice, and patience. What matters is to continue learning, stay organized, and give yourself enough time to improve.

It is important to trust your own ability, especially during moments when you are unsure of yourself. Making mistakes does not mean that you are incapable. Mistakes are a natural part of learning and often provide an opportunity to understand something more clearly.

Instead of allowing a mistake to discourage you, try to see it as a realization of what needs to be improved. A simple “Oh, now I understand where I went wrong” can be an important step forward. Each mistake can teach something valuable, and each attempt provides another opportunity to improve.

Most importantly, remember to recognize your own progress. It is easy to focus on the things that still need improvement and overlook the things that have already been accomplished.

It is natural to compare yourself with others, especially when someone seems to understand something more quickly. However, everyone learns differently and progresses at a different pace.

Someone else’s progress does not make your own progress less meaningful. There may be times when you move quickly and other times when you need more time. What matters is continuing to move forward in a way that works for you.

Having people who genuinely celebrate your achievements without seeing them as a competition is something to appreciate.

“To have a circle that celebrates your success without feeling threatened by it is a blessing not everyone gets to experience.”

Good relationships are not built only on shared successes. They are also built through encouragement, support, understanding, and being happy for one another. Whenever possible, be that kind of person for others as well.

records.content:
Asking for help is not something to be ashamed of. When something is difficult to understand, it is perfectly reasonable to ask a classmate, a friend, or a professor for clarification.

Sometimes, a concept becomes easier simply because someone explains it from a different perspective. Asking questions also shows a willingness to understand rather than simply looking for an answer.

There is a difference between seeking help to learn and taking a shortcut without understanding the work. When help is available, make use of it and take the opportunity to learn from the people around you.

Learning is not only about what happens inside the classroom. The people met along the way can also become an important part of the experience.

Take the time to get to know classmates, work together, help one another, and appreciate the small moments that happen along the way. Some friendships may last for many years, while others may only be part of a particular class, project, or chapter of life. Either way, they can still make the experience more meaningful.

Sometimes, having someone to share the difficult moments and small achievements with can make things feel a little easier.

AI has become a common part of learning and working today, and it can be a useful tool when used responsibly. It can help explain difficult concepts, provide another perspective, identify possible mistakes, or assist when you are unsure where to begin.

However, it is important not to let AI replace the learning process. Read the explanations, ask questions, verify the information, and make an effort to understand the work rather than simply copying an answer.

Use AI as an assistant, not as a replacement for your own understanding.

Be patient with yourself.

There will be times when things go well and times when they do not. There may be moments when you feel confident, and others when you feel uncertain or behind. These experiences are all part of learning.

You will make mistakes. You will encounter things you do not understand. You may even have moments when you question whether you are doing enough. But with time, practice, and persistence, there will also be moments when something finally makes sense.

Those moments are worth remembering.

You do not have to be perfect. Keep learning, trust yourself, appreciate the people who support you, and give yourself the opportunity to grow.
